problem: Which of the following is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation?

examples.problem:
Determine whether the following equation is a first-order linear ODE:

$$
x^2\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}
+
\sin(2x)y
=
e^x.
$$
examples.worked_solution:
We attempt to write the equation in the standard form

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}
+
P(x)y
=
Q(x) \,.
$$

Dividing the equation through by $x^2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)y & ={e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{{x}^{2}}y & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that this equation is now in standard form with $P(x) = \dfrac{\sin{2x}}{x^2}$ and $Q(x) = \dfrac{e^x}{x^2}.$

Because the equation can be written in standard form, we conclude that it is a first-order linear ODE.

feedback.problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{2}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2}={(1-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2}\,.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{2}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2} & ={(1-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2} \\ \frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{2}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2} & =1+{y}^{2}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2}-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{dy}{dx} & =1-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{dy}{dx}+{{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}\,y & ={{1}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=1.$
